newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian students march over poll "fraud".
newsitem.headline: Serbian students march over poll "fraud".

text.p: Serbian students launched another day of street protests in the Serbian capital on Friday over what they say is massive electoral fraud, despite a public holiday and deteriorating winter weather.

Student marches have preceded wider opposition demonstrations every day over the past week amid public outrage over moves by President Slobodan Milosevic's government to annul opposition victories in local elections on November 17.

Friday's march, which appeared to be smaller than previous days, went ahead despite a national Republic Day holiday and fog. Economics professor Ljubomir Madzar said it was shameful that more people were not joining them.
"I admire the minds and courage of these young people who have dared to protest," Madzar told Reuters.
"Every citizen of this country should give his little contribution to bring our society to the level of other democratic societies in Europe and to help us get out of this Balkan darkness."
But he, like many activists, also warned the protesters that they would have to be patient.
"This is part of a long process of societal change. This is an investment in future elections," he said. Serbia's republican parliament is due to face elections next year.
But Western states have expressed serious concern over Milosevic's respect for democratic elections, local or otherwise.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said it was "extremely concerned" about irregularities and shortcomings during federal and municipal polls held earlier this month.
The OSCE added the integrity of the entire election process remained under question until an independent review could be undertaken and said it was ready to help if required.
Publicly opposition leaders insisted that if their supporters could put up with the driving rain that washed protests earlier in the week, they would come in strength even on a public holiday.

Privately though, activists for the opposition coalition Zajedno (Together) said they faced an uphill battle to maintain the momentum of the past week, in which between 50,000 and 100,000 people jammed the city streets daily.
Earlier, one Zajedno leader, Zoran Djindjic, said the coalition had shattered the aura of Milosevic's invincibility, and would capitalise on that in forthcoming elections.
The coalition said it planned to keep the demonstrations rolling at least to Tuesday, when the Serbian parliament is due to convene.
Then they say Zajedno will surround the parliament with what they hope will be their biggest protest yet, to add weight to demands that the parliament recognise their "stolen" local election wins.
But political analysts doubt whether the opposition has the numbers to topple Milosevic, and point to the consistent size of the rallies as an indicator that support had peaked.
They say Milosevic appears to be gambling that the demonstrators will eventually grow tired of daily protests in winter temperatures.
Diplomats say Milosevic has now shattered any surviving democratic credentials he may have had by moving to gag media coverage of the protests.

Belgrade's independent radio station B-92 accused the authorities of jamming its reporting on the rallies, while journalists from independent and state-backed newspapers have complained of attempts to censor their coverage of the protests.
Radio B-92 also said the authorities had shut down private radio stations in the town of Cacak that had been re-broadcasting its news service, citing "licence irregularities."
